Extort
ĕks-tort´
v. (to wrest from a man by force, threat or the abuse of an office)
Latin extorquere, to twist out, from ex-, out, and torquere, to twist. The AV's extortioner is a standing category, and it is listed among sins that bar from the kingdom.

Biblical Definition

To extort is to twist a thing out of a man. Paul makes the extortioner a case for church discipline: “if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat” (1Co 5:11), and lists the same among those who “shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (1Co 6:10). The Lord finds it inside religious scruple: “ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess” (Mat 23:25). The Pharisee thanks God he is not one (Luk 18:11). And John's counsel to the publicans is exact: “Exact no more than that which is appointed you” (Luk 3:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines extort as to draw from by force or compulsion; to wrest or wring from by physical force, by menace, duress, authority, or by any illegal means.

expand to see more

EXTORT, v.t. To draw from by force or compulsion; to wrest or wring from by physical force, by menace, duress, violence, authority, or by any illegal means.

Conquerors extort contributions from the vanquished.

EXTORTION, n. The act of extorting; the act or practice of wresting any thing from a person by force, duress, menaces, authority, or by any undue exercise of power.

Key Scripture

1Co 5:11 — "But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat."

1Co 6:10 — "Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God."

Mat 23:25 — "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess."

Luk 18:11 — "The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican."

Luk 3:13 — "And he said unto them, Exact no more than that which is appointed you."

Modern Corruption

Extortion is imagined as a criminal act, and Webster names its ordinary instrument: the undue exercise of power.

expand to see more

Webster's phrase is the one to keep: extortion is wresting a thing from a person by force, duress, menaces, authority, or by any undue exercise of power. The last clause covers most actual cases. The publicans John addressed were not robbers; they held a lawful office with a lawful right to collect, and the extortion consisted in taking more than was appointed while remaining entirely within the system. His counsel to them is correspondingly narrow — not leave your trade, but exact no more than that which is appointed you.

First Corinthians 5:11 is startling for where it puts the extortioner: in a list with the fornicator and the idolater, as a man a church may not eat with. Financial oppression is treated as a disciplinable offence of the same order as sexual sin, which is not how most congregations rank things. An employer squeezing wages, a lender exploiting desperation, a family member using a will as leverage — each is in Paul's category, and each is usually handled in churches as a private matter rather than as a case.

Matthew 23:25 lands it where it is least expected. The scrupulous men who tithed mint and anise are told that within, the cup is full of extortion and excess — the scruple and the extortion in the same person, and the scruple functioning as the cover. That is the commonest form the sin takes among religious people. It does not present as greed; it presents as prudence, as good management, as holding someone to what was agreed, and the man doing it is often the one most confident that his outside is clean.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek harpax (G727), an extortioner, a ravener; harpage (G724), extortion, plunder; prasso (G4238), to exact, collect; akrasia (G192), excess.

expand to see more

Greek harpax (G727) — extortioner, rapacious; 1 Corinthians 5:10–11, 6:10, Luke 18:11; and of wolves, Matthew 7:15.

Greek harpage (G724) — extortion, plunder; Matthew 23:25, Luke 11:39, Hebrews 10:34.

Greek meden pleon…prassete (G4238) — exact no more; Luke 3:13.

Usage

"“Exact no more than that which is appointed you” — keep the office, change the practice."

"“With such an one no not to eat” — the extortioner, in that list."

"“Within they are full of extortion” — and they tithed mint."
